name: exec_robot_create_thread
description:
Drives the robot along the path already generated for it by trace_targets. Returns immediately -- it posts the request and the tracking bench does the driving. Call wait_for_robot afterwards to find out how it ended.

Returns one of:
- "Started controller thread for robot <id>"
- "Path for specific robot doesn't exist. Generate path first"
- "No robot is attached to this service — start the bench with --rpc before asking anything to drive."
- "Selected ID doesn't exist (<ids>)"

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

robot_padding.description: Accepted and ignored. This rig has one robot, so there is nothing to keep clear of. Default: 30.

name: stop_robot_thread
description: Stops the robot. The bench disarms on its next tick and the ball coasts briefly to a halt.

robot_id.description: Robot ID whose drive should be stopped.

join_timeout.description: Accepted and ignored -- there is no thread to join. Default: 5.0.

name: wait_for_robot
description:
Waits for the current drive to finish and reports HOW it ended. Always call this after exec_robot_create_thread instead of polling get_robot_state, which wastes calls on round trips.

IMPORTANT: a robot stops for four different reasons and only one is success -- it arrived, it gave up stuck, the tracker lost the ball, or a person stopped it. Read 'arrived', not the fact that it stopped.

Returns {"arrived": bool, "outcome": str, "reason": str, "timed_out": bool}. When outcome is 'stuck' the ball is against a boundary; a goal further from the edge is worth trying. When outcome is 'refused' the rig would not start at all and 'reason' says why -- a mirrored camera frame or a missing calibration cannot be fixed by retrying.

timeout_s.description: Seconds to wait before giving up. Default: 30.

name: get_robot_position
description:
Where the tracker last saw the robot, in arena pixels.

Returns {"tracked": false, "reason": ...} when the ball is not currently visible -- a missing robot means 'not seen', never 'has not moved'. When tracked, 'theta' is the direction of TRAVEL rather than which way the robot faces (a Sphero is a sphere and has no visible facing); 'theta_is_measured' is false when the ball is at rest and the bearing is being held from its last motion, and 'theta_age_s' says how old that held bearing is.

name: get_robot_state
description: Returns 'moving' or 'halt'. Prefer wait_for_robot -- 'halt' says the robot stopped but not whether it arrived.

name: orbit
description:
Drives a real circle around a point, repeating until stopped. Use this whenever the ask is to orbit, circle, go around, or loop -- NOT trace_targets, which can only express a list of waypoints and so turns a circle into a polygon with corners.

This never arrives and wait_for_robot will time out on it. Call stop_robot_thread to end it.

Keep the whole circle inside the arena: the centre plus the radius must stay at least 100 pixels from every edge.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

x.description: Centre x in arena pixels. Get the arena size from get_arena — do not assume it.

y.description: Centre y in arena pixels. Get the arena size from get_arena — do not assume it.

radius.description: Radius in arena pixels (10 pixels is 1cm). If the user did not ask for a particular size, use about 80% of the 'max_radius' that get_arena reports -- an orbit is meant to go round the arena, not trace a small circle in the middle of it. Never exceed max_radius: the whole circle must stay inside 'safe'.

name: patrol
description:
Patrols back and forth between two points until stopped. Use this for any 'patrol', 'back and forth', 'sweep' or 'guard the edge' request.

DO NOT build a patrol out of waypoints with trace_targets. An out-and-back route lays both legs on the same line, the follower cannot tell them apart, and the ball reverses early and oscillates around one end instead of covering the run.

This never arrives and wait_for_robot will time out on it. Call stop_robot_thread to end it.

Keep both ends at least 100 pixels from every edge.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

x1.description: First end, x in arena pixels.

y1.description: First end, y in arena pixels.

x2.description: Second end, x in arena pixels.

y2.description: Second end, y in arena pixels.

name: set_trajectory
description: Drives an explicit list of [x, y] waypoints in order, with no path planner in between. trace_targets runs A* and may move a goal it judges unreachable; this drives exactly the shape given, so use it when the shape itself matters. Needs at least two points. Reports arrival through wait_for_robot like an ordinary drive.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

points.description: Waypoints as [[x, y], [x, y], ...] in arena pixels.

name: follow
description:
Chases a point, and keeps chasing it as you move it. Call again with a new x, y to move the target under a ball already on its way -- that updates the goal rather than starting a fresh drive.

NOTE: nothing on this rig can pick a target by itself. Object detection needs SAM2 and a lit room while the ball tracker needs the room dark, and there is only one robot, so there is no second one to chase. You supply the coordinates.

Call stop_robot_thread to stop.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

name: set_flow
description:
Drives a curve you describe with a short expression, instead of listing its points. Use this for shapes a waypoint list says badly -- a figure eight, a spiral, a lissajous, a rose -- and for a 'flow' or 'pattern' request.

Write Python that assigns a list of (x, y) to `points`, in ARENA PIXELS. Available names: cx, cy (the arena centre, whatever get_arena reports), width, height, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, and maths including sin, cos, pi, sqrt. No imports, no attribute access, no while loops, one second.

Figure eight around the centre:
  points = [(cx + 400*sin(2*pi*i/64), cy + 200*sin(4*pi*i/64)) for i in range(64)]

Spiral outwards:
  points = [(cx + 4*i*cos(i/6), cy + 4*i*sin(i/6)) for i in range(80)]

Every point must stay 100 pixels inside the arena or the whole curve is refused -- the ball has width and reads its own position badly near a wall. With closed=true (the default) it repeats until stopped and never arrives; with closed=false it drives the curve once and arrives.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

expression.description: Python assigning a list of (x, y) arena-pixel points to `points`.

closed.description: True to loop the curve until stopped (default), false to drive it once.

name: get_arena
description:
Returns the arena's real size, centre and safe bounds in arena pixels. ALWAYS call this before placing any coordinate, and never assume the arena's dimensions or centre: it is four corners somebody clicked mapped through a camera calibration, and it changes whenever either is redone. It already has -- a re-click moved the centre from (694, 554) to (712, 613).

Returns width, height, centre, max_radius, px_per_cm, width_cm, height_cm, and 'safe' as [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max]. Keep every point of every path inside 'safe' or the drive is refused: the ball has width and reads its own position badly near a wall.

Returns {"known": false, "reason": ...} when the bench has not reported yet.

'max_radius' is the largest circle that fits from the centre without leaving 'safe'. Use about 80% of it for an unqualified 'orbit'.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

name: move_to_cm
description:
Drives to a position given in CENTIMETRES from the arena's top-left corner. x runs right, y runs down — the same way the camera sees it. Use this whenever the user names a position in centimetres; use trace_targets only when you need the path planner to route around something.

Call get_arena first if you need to know how big the arena is in centimetres. Reports arrival through wait_for_robot like an ordinary drive.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

x_cm.description: Centimetres right of the arena's left edge.

y_cm.description: Centimetres down from the arena's top edge.

name: move_by_cm
description:
Moves a distance in a compass direction: "north", "NE", "east", or a number of degrees clockwise from north. North is the TOP of the arena and east is the right.

This is an absolute direction in the room, not relative to the robot. Do not use it for 'forward' or 'ahead': a Sphero is a sphere with no visible facing, so there is no forward for it to have. If the user asks for 'forward', ask which direction they mean.

Refuses if the destination would leave the safe box.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

distance_cm.description: How far to move, in centimetres.

direction.description: north, NE, east, SE, south, SW, west, NW — or degrees clockwise from north.

name: start_scale_run
description:
STEP ONE of calibrating centimetres. Drives the robot in a straight line for a few seconds and reports how far the CAMERA thinks it went.

This needs a person. The camera measures the distance in pixels precisely, but only a tape measure can say what that is in real centimetres. Report the returned 'camera_says_cm' to the user, ask them to measure how far the ball actually travelled, and then call set_measured_distance with the number THEY give you.

The ball coasts after the motors cut, so this measures to where it came to REST. Tell the user to measure to where it stopped, not to where it stopped driving.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.

seconds.description: How long to drive. Default 3. Longer is more accurate but needs more clear floor.

name: set_measured_distance
description:
STEP TWO of calibrating centimetres. Takes the distance the USER measured with a tape, folds the correction into the camera calibration, and saves it — so every later run starts already scaled and this does not need repeating.

Only call this with a number the user gave you. Never estimate it yourself: the entire point is that the camera cannot know this and a person can. If the user has not given you a measurement, ask for one.

measured_cm.description: The distance the user measured, in centimetres.

robot_id.description: Robot ID. This rig has one robot and its id is 2.
